qt: to the Commission Fernand Kartheiser (NI) Subject:

A new study by the Technical University of Munich (TUM) has exposed major flaws in how the EU regulates CO2 emissions from passenger cars1. The core problem is that EU rules focus on tailpipe emissions, rather than considering a vehicle’s entire life cycle. Led by professors Johannes Fottner, Magnus Fröhling and Tim Büthe, the study analysed vehicles’ climate footprints across their life cycle, from production and use to disposal, which the Commission’s current approach does not account for. It found that the life cycle CO2 emissions of battery-electric vehicles are, on average, only 41 % lower than those of combustion engine vehicles. Yet EU rules treat them as ‘zeroemission’. This miscalculation could have adverse economic and environmental consequences. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this study, and if so, does it intend to address the flaws the study underlines in the current EU regulatory approach?
Will the Commission now revise how emissions targets and penalties are calculated to take account of emissions throughout a vehicle’s entire life cycle?
If so, does the Commission intend to amend Regulation (EU) 2019/6312 to mandate verified life cycle emissions reporting for passenger cars?

at: EN on behalf of the Commission (30.10.2026) Greenhouse gas emissions occur across the full lifecycle of a vehicle, from extraction of materials to end of life. The Commission is aware of the Technical University of Munich paper, the findings of which in fact confirm that battery-electric vehicles significantly reduce lifecycle emissions (in c. 92% of scenarios), and highlights that the automotive industry does not support introducing binding lifecycle assessment obligations. The CO2 emission performance standards1 are part of a wider instrument mix that covers the entire supply chain. The standards regulate vehicle manufacturers and provide the necessary level of regulatory certainty to facilitate compliance. It is important that there is a clear allocation of responsibility to ensure that each actor in the supply chain is accountable for delivering the emissions reductions that it is best placed to achieve. The standards already include a provision for voluntary reporting of lifecycle emissions to limit the administrative burden for industry. As part of the automotive package of December 2025, the Commission has made a proposal2 to revise the standards which is being discussed by the co-legislators. It proposes a pragmatic approach beyond tailpipe emissions by recognising CO₂ savings achieved elsewhere, including through the decarbonisation of fuels and steel. A methodology for legislative compliance based on lifecycle assessment would require harmonisation of many assumptions which significantly influence the results and which would determine compliance requirements. This could take years to establish, creating uncertainty while increasing the complexity of the legal framework and reporting burden, countering the simplification objectives.
